newsitem.title: BOSNIA: World Bank urges rapid privatisation in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: World Bank urges rapid privatisation in Bosnia.

text.p: Reconstruction aid flowing to Bosnia has created an initial economic boost but privatisation reforms must be adopted soon or the country could squander its chance at recovery, the World Bank said on Thursday.

Despite appeals from international financial authorities, the country's autonomous Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic have yet to adopt Western-style privatisation policies some 18 months after the end of the 1992-95 war.

The World Bank and other foreign experts were pushing for adoption of privatisation laws within four weeks, in part to coincide with a fund-raising conference for reconstruction aid expected to be held this month.
"We are recommending the most rapid privatisation possible," Rory O'Sullivan, director of the World Bank in Bosnia, told Reuters.
Some $2 billion in reconstruction aid committed last year helped produce a 50 percent growth rate in the Moslem-Croat federation, which covers half the country.

The Serb entity has experienced slower growth because the international community linked aid to compliance with the 1995 peace treaty. As a result, the Serbs have lost out on most of the post-war aid so far.
The World Bank estimates the economy will grow at a 30 to 35 percent rate this year but says that the peacetime recovery will stumble without sweeping privatisation reforms.
Privatisation legislation, which was drawn up by Price Waterhouse consultants, has been held up in the Moslem-Croat federation parliament due to political quarrels between Moslem and Croat deputies.
The World Bank was concerned that an important draft law, which defines the value of state-owned companies, had been stuck in parliament for months, O'Sullivan said.
Political analysts say the federation finance minister, Drago Bilandzija, had blocked adoption of the "open balance sheet" law partly because of a dispute over privatisation of enterprises.

Bilandzija and other Croat deputies were opposed to allowing large numbers of Moslem war veterans and police to use passbooks to obtain shares in privatised enterprises. Bosnian army soldiers and police were issued passbooks last year as credit for unpaid salaries.

Once the federation adopts the legislation, "small-scale privatisation" should proceed quickly, foreign experts said. The law would allow the sale of companies with less than 50 employees and assets valued at less than 500,000 German marks ($290,000).
Bosnia's Serb republic has adopted privatisation laws which foreign experts say still needed to signicant amendments to attract investors.

The World Bank has called for Serb authorities to raise the 15 percent share offered to private investors in state-owned companies and to reduce the role of state investment funds in the privatisation process.

O'Sullivan said donor countries have pledged $5 billion in reconstruction aid for Bosnia over a period of three to four years but that amount represented a "fraction" of what the Bosnian economy required to return to its pre-war level.
Only privatisation would bring in the $30 billion necessary to return the economy back to health, he said.
"We need the privatisation laws to go through, this is what is going to bring in foreign direct investment," he said.
